title: "Figures and reports"

## Reporting

Two documents, each one self-contained HTML file.

**The one-page report** is the scores, the run and a few figures, small enough to send:

```r
write_results(res, "results/")
report(res, "report.html", group = "condition")
```

It is one file, inlined CSS, base64 figures, the table embedded, so it still works after somebody
emails it, which is the only thing anybody does with a report.

**The full run, step by step.** `run_report()` runs quality control, scoring, technical error,
prediction intervals, age acceleration, a consensus test across clocks when a group column is
named, and the interpretation tables, and writes every deliverable into one directory: the same
directory the `report` command writes. With `quarto = TRUE` it adds `falconage_report.qmd`, in which
every file of that directory sits under the step that produced it, in the order a reader has to
take them, because each step is only as reliable as the ones before it:

| Step | What it holds |
|---|---|
| 0. Provenance | versions, the coefficient file and SHA-256 behind each clock, precision, warnings |
| 1. Input and quality control | per-sample missingness and beta distribution; the QC figures |
| 2. Coverage | per-clock coverage by feature count and by coefficient weight; clocks not scored, and why |
| 3. Scores | the scores, what each category of clock measures, and how the clocks relate |
| 4. Agreement with chronological age | error against age and whether it depends on age |
| 5. Uncertainty | technical standard error and conformal prediction intervals |
| 6. Age acceleration | residuals on age, for the scales where they are defined |
| 7. Group comparison | the consensus verdict and the test for every clock |
| 8. Interpretation | what each score means and the published evidence, with DOIs |
| 9. Further outputs | every other file in the directory, named and sized |

A file the report does not recognise still appears, in step 9, so nothing in the directory is
left out. Tables expand, search, page and download as CSV; figures enlarge on click and download
at full resolution. Rendered, it is one HTML file with every figure and table embedded: 3.7 MB for
16 samples and three clocks.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
fa.report.run_report(d, "results/", group_col="condition", quarto=True)
```

### R

```r
run_report(d, "results/", group = "condition", quarto = TRUE)
```

### Command line

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu \
  report betas.csv --outdir results/ --group-col condition --quarto
```

:::

**Rendering it.** Quarto is not in the FALCONAge image. Installed it takes 423 MB, which would add
about 17% to the 2.5 GB image for an optional document, so inside the image the source is written and
the run says so. Render it with the Quarto container, from the output directory, and open
`falconage_report.html`:

```bash
cd results
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w \
  ghcr.io/quarto-dev/quarto quarto render falconage_report.qmd
```

Where Quarto is installed, `run_report()` renders it directly, and `quarto_report("results/")`
(R) or `fa.report.write_quarto_report("results/", render=True)` (Python) rewrites the report for
a directory that already exists.

## Plots

### What FALCONAge draws

Thirty-two figures in Python, twenty-one of them also in R, drawn alike because both languages
read their colours, titles, subtitles and one-line descriptions from the same `colorscheme.yaml`.
The [gallery](figures.qmd) shows every one. The coverage map is drawn first on every run, before
any clock is scored, and cannot be switched off. Every function returns its
data frame as well as its figure, which is how two rendering engines draw the same numbers.

**Ready for a manuscript.** A figure carries its axes and its legend and nothing else: no title,
no subtitle and no caption on the canvas, so it drops into a panel layout as it is. Each one is
written as a pair named after its title, with the clock appended for per-clock figures:

```
figures/predicted_against_chronological_age_horvath2013.png
figures/predicted_against_chronological_age_horvath2013.txt
```

The `.txt` holds the title, the figure's own numbers (n, r, MedAE and the like) and the
description, ready to paste into a figure legend. `save_figure()` writes a pair from any figure
you draw yourself, in Python (`fa.plot.save_figure(fig, "figures")`) and in R
(`save_figure(p, "figures")`); `figure_text()` returns the same text as a list. Both reports show
the title and description beneath each figure and link its `.txt`.

| Figure | Answers |
|---|---|
| `clock_coverage_manhattan` | where every clock's CpGs sit on the genome, which ones the data carries, and which clocks share them |
| `ba_vs_ca` | does this clock track age here, and with what bias |
| `bland_altman` | is the error age-dependent (regression dilution made visible) |
| `calibration` | is the predicted age calibrated across the age range |
| `acceleration_by_group` | do cases accelerate relative to controls |
| `acceleration_density` | the same, as distributions rather than summaries |
| `acceleration_heatmap` | clock × study, the whole pooled picture in one panel |
| `forest` | effect size with an interval, per clock |
| `clock_corr` | which clocks agree, clustered |
| `clock_chord` | how much of that agreement is shared CpGs rather than shared signal |
| `clock_radar` | one profile per group across clocks, on a common z scale |
| `clock_pca`, `clock_embedding` | sample structure in clock space; ageotypes |
| `clock_scatter_matrix` | pairwise acceleration, the `plot_baa` layout |
| `coverage_bar`, `missingness` | which clocks are scoring imputed values, read before the scores |
| `beta_density` | is the beta distribution bimodal, or did normalisation break |
| `sex_check` | does the X/Y dosage match the recorded sex |
| `platform_comparison`, `study_comparison` | is the batch bigger than the biology |
| `benchmark_bars`, `benchmark_error_bias`, `benchmark_heatmap` | AA1/AA2, the MedAE–MedE tradeoff, clock × dataset |
| `timecourse`, `trajectory` | clocks across a timepoint variable |
| `clock_atlas` | every clock, every pooled study, one figure |

`clock_chord` is the one with no precedent in the list above and it earns its place: the
correlation heatmap says two clocks agree, and the chord says how much of that agreement was
built in by construction. A pair with a thick chord and a high correlation has told you much less
than a pair with a high correlation and no chord at all.

A volcano plot of clock associations is implemented (`fa.plot.volcano`, R `plot_volcano`). GSEA (11)
belongs to feature-level biology rather than to scoring, and spatial maps (12) wait on the spatial
modality.

Two rules the code enforces rather than recommends. A figure whose data is empty, flat, or all
zeros raises `NothingToPlot` and `save_all` records the reason, because an axis-free rectangle in
a report reads as a measurement of nothing rather than as an absence of measurement. And the
scale-type gate applies to figures too: a `pace_ratio` clock never reaches an acceleration panel.
